title: Same world, different senses
text:
Frontier AI models are becoming more capable every year. They’re trained on a massive corpus of data and then post-trained to be conversational and perform certain tasks. More interestingly, given a few examples, we saw that they can do tasks even if they weren’t trained on them! This is called in-context learning (ICL).
The models are trained on petabyte-scale (if not more) multi-modal data from different sources across the internet, as well as sources from specialized domains, such as biology. Since these models are becoming larger and larger and trained on more data and tasks, they’re beginning to have a deeper understanding of our world and a certain projection of reality. This leads to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.


If we think about it, the data on the internet is the projection of our own reality. We write about our trips to China, we post selfies on social networks with our pets and we share information on the internet. The images in their raw (R, G, B) form or text we write are imitations of our experiences, knowledge and world.
Let’s take a vision model that has been trained across huge corpora of images on the internet to detect an object on an unseen image. Or a language model that’s been trained to predict the next token for a given sequence of words. The more we scale these models, the more they start to have an accurate representation of our reality. This is what the Platonic Representation Hypothesis states: that the models trained on different data and modalities begin to converge to a shared statistical model of our reality in their own representation spaces.




  Larger models project closer to the world
  Arrows from one origin. A horizontal arrow is the world. Each model is an arrow that is longer and points closer to the world than the one before: early LLMs, GPT-3, Opus 4.5, and a hypothetical GPT-6-Astra. Dashed lines drop from each tip onto the world axis. Bars below show that each projection covers more of the world.

Figure 1: A thought experiment. Each arrow is a model’s representation of the world. Larger models point closer to the world, so their projection covers more of it.



The question being: When will we converge? How large do we need to scale? If scaling current models is sufficient to come to the closest representation of the real world to solve currently open problems, e.g. autonomous driving, then it certainly isn’t efficient. We’re investing hundreds of billions of dollars into capital, energy and human resources to power these models.
One of the most influential scientists in machine learning, Yann LeCun, believes the opposite. He argues that LLMs do not possess the human common sense from the text alone, since we also experience other modalities, such as visual, aural and spatial sense (LeCun 2022). Through interactions and experiences with the physical world, we’ve intuitively learned the capability to perceive and predict the consequences of our actions, such as pushing a cup off the table makes it drop to the ground. That’s how babies learn about gravity. LeCun argues that text and language is a lossy description of the real world and a low-bandwidth means of transporting information. This is why he and his team at Meta AI developed JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture). But that’s for another blog post.



Last week, Takehi et al. (2026) showed that models can read, write and modify neural network weights. They gave the weights of the network in a text form, along with some other environment information and asked which game the network was trained on. This really excited me. In some sense, it even inspired me to write this. When I first learned of neural networks, it blew me away that these weights which are just numbers can figure out complex problems. On their own, the weights don’t make any sense. That’s exactly why the field of interpretability and explainable AI (XAI) is booming right now. Models, which are themselves neural networks, can optimize neural network weights! It’s like neurosurgery: surgeons, or rather the surgeon’s brain, operating on a patient’s brain. I believe this is a step towards recursive self-improvement.
But I wondered, if GPT-6-Astra can make sense of the neural network weights, can it make sense of other nonsensical-to-human data? That question led me to the following experiments.

title: Matija Akrap
text:
I am a Data Science master’s student at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing (FER), University of Zagreb. For the 2026/27 academic year I am on exchange at KU Leuven.
I am interested in machine learning, more specifically deep learning and natural language processing. It is important to achieve an understanding and interpretability of how frontier AI models are trained, on how they think, reason and make decisions, ensuring that their internal processes are transparent, reliable, and aligned with human values.

Research
Detecting Evasive Answers in Political Interviews · Oct 2025 – Jun 2026
SemEval-2026 Task 6, research project in the Project R course, FER · Zagreb, Croatia

Compared flat, hierarchical and multitask RoBERTa models, with the hierarchical model performing best.
Found that multitask models broke the label hierarchy, and enforcing it at inference raised F1.

Personal Language Model · PyTorch, QLoRA, mlx-lm · GitHub

Pre-trained a GPT-style model from scratch, then QLoRA fine-tuned Ministral-8B to write in my style.

Led a 7-person team building a social platform for rating, tracking and recommending films and shows.
Built a hybrid recommender combining PyTorch matrix factorization with genre embeddings on 23.6M ratings.
Solved user cold start by mapping genre picks into the embedding space, with pgvector and fuzzy-logic ranking.

Last Translation Benchmark · contributor · Paper
